title: The Sikligar Sikhs
hookLine: a community of metalworkers, many living in poverty

lines: A GRINDING WHEEL AT THE MARKET'S EDGE.
A SMALL FORGE, A CART, A ROAD.
A TRADE THAT ONCE SERVED THE GURUS.
cards: A grinding wheel spins at the edge of a market, throwing a thin fan of sparks. A man in a worn turban holds a kitchen knife to it, turns it, tests the edge on his thumbnail, hands it back.
Next to him, a boy fans the coals under a small forge. By evening they'll pack the wheel, the tools and the bedding onto a cart and move on. Shoppers pass without looking twice.
They may not know that this family's trade, in Sikh tradition, once served the Gurus' own armies. They are Sikligar Sikhs.

teach.b: The Sikligars are a community of metalworkers. Their crafts are forging, sharpening and mending: blades, locks, cooking griddles, iron tools of every kind.

teach.h: TRADITION: SMITHS FOR THE GURUS' ARMIES.
teach.b: Tradition links their ancestors to the years when the Gurus raised armed companies, and remembers Sikligar smiths making weapons for them.
Over time, Sikligar families took to the road, moving from town to town with their tools.
Today Sikligar families can face deep poverty. Work is irregular, schooling is hard to keep when a family moves, and a craft that once forged swords now sharpens kitchen knives for small coins.
They hold to Sikh identity, the Guru, the turban, the gurdwara, often while living at the edges of the towns they serve.
Some Sikh groups and volunteers now work alongside Sikligar communities on schooling, housing and health.

teach.h: ANG 1245: EARN BY LABOR, GIVE BY HAND.
teach.b: Guru Nanak, in a salok on Ang 1245, says in paraphrase: whoever eats what they earn by their own labor, and gives some of it with their own hand, has recognized the way.
Hold that line up against the man at the grinding wheel. He earns by the work of his hands, as plainly as anyone can, and the Guru's words honor exactly that life.
And the line doesn't stop at earning: give some of it with your own hand. That half is asked of everyone who hears it, the man at the wheel and the one handing him a knife.
In tradition's telling, the Sikligars kept the Gurus' steel sharp in hard years. Remembering them now isn't charity from above. It's the panth remembering one of its own.

how: Sikligar Sikhs work as smiths and sharpeners, often moving with their tools; some Sikh groups and volunteers work with Sikligar communities on schooling, housing and health.

games.q: Guru Nanak's salok on Ang 1245 describes someone who has recognized the way. what do they do?
o: earn by their own labor and give some of it with their own hand.
give up work and live on gifts.
games.why: earn by your own labor, and give some of it with your own hand: such a one has recognized the way.

practice: Bring to mind one person who works hard and still struggles, someone who fixes, cleans, delivers or carries, and see their hands at work.
Breathe in the question of one real thing you could do for them, a fair price paid without bargaining, a proper thank-you, and breathe out, keeping the answer. If you pray, rest on Waheguru.
